wa_walking_legend_wall.blurb: A tall face just right of the Wart in the Lower Lump at Index, on the Skykomish Valley side of the Cascades. Twelve routes mix sport and trad, with sport lines in the majority and a handful of easier gear climbs. Difficulty runs from about 5.7 up to the low 5.11s, with most routes sitting around 5.10. The stone is featured and the wall is steeper than the nearby Beetle Bailey Slab. Forest at the base keeps it well shaded, which helps on warm days. A short walk from the road and tracks puts you at the start, so it suits a quick session.

wa_wall_of_many_faces.blurb: The main wall of the Oasis crag along the Tieton River in south-central Washington. A dozen routes, nearly all sport, run from 5.8 to about 5.12, and most fall in the 5.10 range, so it is best for climbers comfortable on the middle grades. Rock quality is variable: the lower part is smoother, while higher up the cliff turns to thin columns, and the crag is described as chossier than its Tieton neighbours. A cave marks the base. The sun hits the face for nearly the whole day, which makes it a handy winter option. Expect a hike up a hill from the parking.

wa_white_wall.blurb: A steep sport wall at McLellan Rocks, west of Spokane along the Spokane River. It holds twelve routes, eleven of them sport and one trad, with grades from 5.7 to 5.11. Most lines are in the 5.10 range, so it favours climbers who are past the beginner stage but not yet chasing the hardest McLellan projects. The wall sits on the east side of the canyon, roughly halfway up beyond the pond, and the walk from the pond takes only a couple of minutes. A few easier 5.7 and 5.8 options give newer leaders a place to warm up.

wa_windy_slab.blurb: A small roadside slab in the Columbia Gorge, a few miles east of Stevenson on the Washington side. Twelve short routes, around 45 feet tall, split among sport, trad and top-rope. The climbing is balancy and technical rather than powerful, with grades from easy terrain through the 5.10s and a single 5.11, and the largest share at 5.10. The slab faces the Gorge with views across to Oregon, and wind pours through nearly all the time, so winter days can be cold. Late spring to early fall is the most comfortable window. The top forms a flat terrace that works well for belaying and setting up rappels.

wa_1_shire_wall.blurb: The westernmost wall at Ozone in the Columbia Gorge, and the first one you meet when walking in from the main pullout. Twelve short routes, nearly all trad with a single sport line, ranging from 5.5 to 5.10 with most at 5.6 to 5.9. That makes it a friendly spot for newer gear leaders. The routes are short and can be a bit dirty, and it sees fewer climbers than many neighbouring walls. It is shadier than the crags around it, and Ozone as a whole is well shaded. Bring a standard trad rack.

wa_lost_wall.blurb: A small wall at McLellan Rocks, near Spokane, on the south side of a little canyon with its main face pointing northeast. Twelve routes, ten sport and two trad, run from 5.7 to about 5.11. About half of them sit in the 5.10 range. A few routes cluster on the left side, while others spread out some distance farther right along the base, and several of those further routes are reported as really good. The mix of grades gives intermediate climbers a decent day, and there is a crack at the easy end for those who want gear.

wa_zappa_wall.blurb: A steep, mostly shady wall in the Lookout Point area of Index, on the Skykomish Valley side of the Cascades. Twelve routes, largely trad with a few sport and top-rope options, span about 5.7 to 5.11, and most are around 5.10. The face offers good cracks, some roofs and a bit of slab. It was overlooked for years, and recent cleaning has opened up fresh lines. Most climbs need a lead, though a handful of easy top-rope setups exist. Reaching it means a woodland hike on the trail network beyond Halloween crag, which takes longer than the town walls.
